headline: Verifier soundness caps RL reasoning
summary: New work argues an unsound reward, not compute, is what limits RL for reasoning outside maths and code.
display_body: Recent gains in model reasoning come from reinforcement learning on reasoning traces, but almost entirely in domains that have a cheap, trustworthy checker — a maths answer key, a unit test. The authors call the missing ingredient elsewhere the verification gap, and model it: in a best-of-N setup (generate N answers, keep the one the verifier likes best), the correlation between the verifier and ground truth (ρ) is an exact "exchange rate" between test-time compute and real capability, and an unsound verifier imposes a polynomial penalty as you scale N. In program-synthesis tests with executable ground truth, a weak verifier's soundness collapses under optimization pressure (0.94 → 0.32 at N=4096) — i.e. selection alone "manufactures" apparent quality that is really reward hacking — while a verifier re-anchored to reality keeps improving.
why: it reframes the scaling debate: past the domains with a clean checker, throwing more inference compute at a shaky reward can actively make a model look better while getting worse, and the paper gives a way to measure how much.

headline: 122B coding agent trained in a shell
summary: T1, a 122B MoE trained with RL in a live shell, lifts Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 43.8% to 64.0%.
display_body: T1 is a Mixture-of-Experts model (MoE — only a fraction of the network's "expert" sub-modules fire per token, so a 122B-parameter model runs at a fraction of the compute) trained with RL while operating an actual shell in a cloud sandbox for 300-plus tool-call turns per task, rewarded by executing each task's own test suite. The recipe's substance is in stabilising that training: a dense process reward that scores a trajectory by how many verifiers pass, plus engineering (they call it TITO/R3) to keep the tokens the model trained on aligned with the ones it actually sampled — cutting the train-vs-inference log-probability gap from 0.021 to 0.013. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 the post-training raises the base model from 43.8% to 64.0% of tasks resolved, with training tasks deliberately disjoint from the benchmark to guard against memorisation.
why: long-horizon "do real work in a terminal" agents are exactly the coding-assistant frontier, and this is one of the more complete public recipes for training one with RL rather than prompting a closed model.

headline: Subagents beat loaded skill files
summary: Invoking a skill as a subagent outperforms pasting its instructions into context on long tasks.
display_body: "Agent skills" are reusable capability bundles — instructions, scripts, resources — that an agent normally uses by loading the instructions into its own context window and following them. The paper tests the alternative: invoke the skill as a subagent with a fresh context window instead. It finds subagent execution wins when a skill exposes a clear input→output contract and its instructions actually encode the procedure to fulfil it, because the main agent's reasoning degrades as its context fills up; the cost is extra tokens spent coordinating between the main agent and the subagent.
why: it's a direct, empirical read on an architecture choice practitioners face today (this is the subagents-vs-skills question in tools like Claude Code), and names the specific condition — a clean contract — under which delegation pays for its overhead.

headline: Why post-training quantization works
summary: A mechanistic account: layer errors cancel and output geometry protects the top tokens.
display_body: Post-training quantization stores a trained model's weights at lower precision (e.g. 4-bit) to shrink it, and each rounded weight injects a small error into the model's internal activations. Naively those errors should compound layer by layer and wreck predictions — and in a randomly initialised network they do. The authors ask why they don't in a pretrained one, and find two mechanisms that emerge during pretraining: the error a layer newly adds tends to partially cancel the error it inherited from below, so the discrepancy grows slowly; and the output ("LM-head") geometry preferentially preserves the ranking and probabilities of the top, most-confident tokens.
why: quantization is how large models fit on modest or local hardware, and it has largely been an empirical dark art; a mechanistic account of why it survives suggests where it will break (long chains, low-confidence tokens) rather than leaving it to trial and error.

headline: Synthesized rewards for diagnosis agents
summary: TRACE hides causes in a simulator to make objective rewards, lifting a 35B model above frontier baselines.
display_body: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR — training against an automatic correctness check) works for maths and code but not for diagnosis, where establishing the true cause of an anomaly needs costly expert investigation and may stay ambiguous. TRACE sidesteps that: it samples a hidden intervention, injects it into a controlled simulator, and generates the data that intervention would produce — so the injected cause is the ground-truth label and gives an objective reward, while the agent still has to investigate noisy, confounded evidence with Python and SQL. In a digital-advertising diagnostic environment with 12 root causes, supervised fine-tuning lifts a 35B model from 0.159 to 0.637 full-attribution accuracy, and subsequent RL reaches 0.757 — above every prompted baseline tested, including Claude Opus 5 at 0.686.
why: it's a general trick for extending RLVR into domains where verification is normally expensive — synthesise the world so the answer is known by construction — and shows a mid-size open model overtaking frontier models on the resulting task.

headline: One compressor for any ratio
display_body: Soft context compression squeezes a long context into a handful of "memory tokens" a frozen model reads in place of the raw text. Existing compressors bake the ratio in at training time, so each deployed ratio needs its own model and the same ratio gets applied to every input regardless of need. FlexComp trains one model to work at any ratio (Matryoshka-style: the memory budget is sampled per example during training), then picks the budget per input via confidence-based routing or a lightweight predictor. A single model matches separately trained fixed-ratio specialists, preserves 98%+ accuracy at up to 266× average compression, and at serving scale cuts the KV cache (KV-cache — the stored keys/values that let a model avoid recomputing earlier tokens) by 50% while raising decoding throughput 47%.
why: it turns compression ratio from a fixed deployment decision into a per-request knob, which is the practical difference between one model to serve and a dozen.

headline: Agent hidden states predict success
display_body: As agents move into safety-critical settings, knowing how much to trust an in-progress run matters, but agentic workflows fail in complex ways — bad plans, wrong tool calls, a shifting environment — that surface confidence scores capture poorly. The authors probe the model's internal representations instead: Latent Trajectory Dynamics summarises how the residual stream (the model's running internal activation vector) changes across a trajectory, and an Action Representation Probe reads the state at each action decision. Across Bash, SQL and Python benchmarks and three model families, both beat generation- and sequence-based confidence baselines, giving a zero-overhead reliability monitor that needs no extra prompting or repeated sampling.
why: a cheap "is this run going off the rails?" signal read straight from activations is exactly what you want to gate or halt an autonomous agent before it does damage.

headline: Efficient RL with transition lookahead
display_body: This is a theory result on RL with "transition look-ahead" — the agent may see which states a sequence of ℓ actions would visit before committing. Look-ahead can help a lot, but exact optimal planning with it was known to be NP-hard (computationally intractable at scale) only for discount factors pushed arbitrarily close to 1; it was open whether the hardness was real for ordinary settings. The paper resolves both ends: exact planning stays NP-hard for every fixed discount factor, yet a randomized polynomial-time scheme gets near-optimal for any fixed look-ahead depth, with regret matching classical tabular RL up to log factors even when transitions are unknown.
why: "look before you leap" is a natural upgrade for planning agents; this says you shouldn't chase the exact optimum (it's genuinely hard) but can get essentially all the benefit efficiently.

headline: Dataset of AI-scientist reasoning traces
display_body: Benchmarks for autonomous "AI scientist" agents usually grade only the final artefact — code, a hypothesis, a paper — discarding the reasoning that produced it. OpenDiscoveryTrace releases 558 complete agent trajectories across 124 scientific tasks (drug discovery, materials, genomics, literature analysis), each step recording thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors and self-reported confidence. A striking early finding: three frontier models reach comparable success rates (84–89%), yet the process differs sharply — one model produced roughly 30× more errors than another despite similar final scores.
why: if agents that score the same reason very differently, output-only leaderboards are hiding the failure modes that matter for trusting an agent's work — and a public trace dataset is what lets anyone audit them.

headline: OpenAI opens its Agents API
summary: OpenAI's Agents API enters public beta on the same infrastructure behind Codex and ChatGPT.
display_body: OpenAI opens its Agents API — the plumbing behind Codex and ChatGPT. Now in public beta, it lets developers build cloud agents that run for hours, execute code and process files on the same infrastructure that powers Codex and ChatGPT, with automatic context management, parallel tool use, and delegation to sub-agents. Developers can use OpenAI-hosted sandboxes or partners (Cloudflare, Vercel, Oracle); OpenAI says there are no extra fees beyond token usage, and it builds on the open-source Codex harness with MCP and custom-function support.

headline: GPT-Live-1 adds full-duplex voice
display_body: GPT-Live-1 brings full-duplex voice to the API. OpenAI's new speech API lets an app listen and talk at the same time, rather than the strict turn-taking of earlier voice modes — the substantive change is simultaneous input and output for more natural interruption and back-channel.

headline: Fields medalist launches AI-safety institute
display_body: A Fields medalist launches an institute chasing provable AI safety. Jacob Tsimerman, a 2026 Fields Medal recipient, announced the Mathematical AI Safety Institute (MAISI), an independent research body in the San Francisco Bay Area starting in January 2027 with 10–30 mathematicians; Tsimerman is also joining OpenAI's safety team. The stated ambition — safety you can prove the way cryptographers argue a cipher is unbreakable — is aspirational: as the founders concede, there is not yet even an agreed formal definition of what "safe" means for a model, so treat this as a research agenda, not a delivered method.

headline: DeepSeek open-weights V4.1-Flash
summary: DeepSeek's MIT-licensed V4.1-Flash is a 552B MoE with 1M-token context, built to slash the KV cache and claiming coding parity with closed models.
display_body: DeepSeek releases V4.1-Flash — open weights, 552B, built to make long-context agents cheap. The latest in DeepSeek's V4 open-weights line (distinct from last week's V4-Flash-Vision-Exp), V4.1-Flash is a 552-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model handling up to 1M tokens of context, released under the permissive MIT licence. DeepSeek's stated design goal is shrinking the KV cache — the per-token memory an agent accumulates over many steps, which drives up serving cost — and it reports roughly halving the compute needed to read input versus generate output. On coding tasks DeepSeek says the model matches top closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic, while remaining weaker on complex scientific tasks and image analysis. From 12:00 Beijing time on 2026-09-14, DeepSeek plans to route V4-Pro API requests to V4.1-Flash and retire V4-Pro in an orderly wind-down. Treat the head-to-head coding claim as the vendor's own technical-report figure pending independent evaluation.

headline: Fable 5.1 edges Astra on ErdosBench
summary: On the 226-problem ErdosBench, Fable 5.1 edges GPT-6 Astra by 0.024 in judge-graded research-math.
display_body: On research-grade maths, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra finish in a near dead heat. ErdosBench scores models on 226 Erdős-inspired open maths problems, graded not by raw solve-count but by an external judge on an A–F scale (A = sound and appropriately scoped; C = a material gap; D/F = misleading or contradicted), with model-specific proof audits — a deliberately harder-to-game signal than "problems solved." On the full run, Fable 5.1 (xhigh) leads with a 3.25 judge average (grade mix A=104 / B=112 / C=10, no D/F), edging GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) at 3.23 (A=106 / B=102 / C=18) by 0.024 points — the leaderboard calls it an audit-level tie, with Fable stronger at conservatively-scoped partial work and Astra the better "theorem closer." Both sit well short of saturation: this is a real but modest step on research-math reasoning, not a solved benchmark, and it lands the same week OpenAI moved GPT-6 Astra to general release.

headline: US names six Chinese AI distillers
summary: US agencies allege six Chinese AI firms distilled US frontier models since late 2024.
display_body: US agencies name six Chinese firms over "industrial-scale" model distillation. In a joint release on Tuesday 2026-09-08, the NSA, CISA and FBI alleged that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI have run large-scale efforts since at least late 2024 to distil the capabilities of US frontier models — including variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok — "likely" with "Chinese government awareness." Distillation here means training a model on another model's outputs to copy its behaviour cheaply. Read this as a government allegation, not an adjudicated finding: it is the agencies' characterisation, the named firms have not been shown to have responded, and "likely" and "awareness" are doing load-bearing work in the claim.

headline: Class action targets Claude usage limits
summary: A class action says Anthropic oversells Claude usage multipliers that apply only within five-hour windows.
display_body: Class action says Claude's usage "multipliers" oversell what subscribers actually get. Plaintiffs allege Anthropic misrepresents its Claude plans — Max at $100/month advertised as 5× Pro usage, $200 as 20× — because the multipliers apply only within rolling five-hour windows and are further capped weekly, so real usage lands well below what buyers expect (per The Verge). Anthropic does document this structure on its help pages and has filed a motion to dismiss, arguing the details were available via hyperlinks at purchase; the plaintiffs counter that customers cannot independently verify what an AI service delivers. For a reader paying for these plans, the concrete takeaway is that the headline multiplier is a within-window figure, not a monthly one.

headline: Anthropic book settlement in disarray
display_body: Anthropic's $1.5bn authors settlement bogs down over who gets paid. The proposed settlement resolving authors' copyright claims against Anthropic has run into disputes among authors and publishers over allocation of the money — a reminder that even a headline settlement figure is not the end of the litigation.
